name: Investigation Station
topics_techniques_covered: demonstrated_achievement
performance/authentic task scored by rubric
open-ended investigation
one_liner: The child designs and runs a short hands-on investigation - like finding which ramp setting makes a ball roll farthest - and their testing strategy and conclusion are scored.
interaction: A simple science sandbox poses a loose question (which ramp makes the ball go farthest?). The child chooses settings (ramp angle, surface, ball), runs trials, watches the outcome measured on screen, and can keep testing before recording a conclusion by picture-menu or text. The engine logs which combinations are tested (breadth), whether successive tests change one thing at a time to be informative, the full test sequence, progress toward the answer over trials, and a rubric score for the reasoning in the final conclusion. There is no single scripted path.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand demo (<=10s) shows a hand setting a low ramp and releasing the ball (short roll), then raising only the ramp and releasing again (longer roll), then tapping the 'it went farther' result - cueing 'try things, watch what happens, then say what you found.' One unscored warm-up trial lets the child run one test before scoring.

learning_science.principle: Authentic performance assessment reveals higher-order reasoning that multiple-choice items cannot elicit
learning_science.why: Designing and carrying out an investigation shows planning, control of variables, and interpretation - process evidence of ability invisible to keyed items
learning_science.concrete_decision: Deliver an open investigation scored by rubric on reasoning and interpretation, not a single correct selection
learning_science.source: Shavelson, R. J., Baxter, G. P., & Pine, J. (1992). Performance assessments: Political rhetoric and measurement reality. Educational Researcher, 21(4), 22-27.

learning_science.principle: The control-of-variables strategy (changing one thing at a time) is a hallmark of early scientific reasoning
learning_science.why: Whether a child spontaneously runs informative, unconfounded tests separates strong young reasoners well before formal science instruction
learning_science.concrete_decision: Score test informativeness - one-variable-at-a-time, disambiguating trials - via the hypothesis-search and exploration logs (M-HYP, M-EXPLORE)
learning_science.source: Klahr, D., & Nigam, M. (2004). The equivalence of learning paths in early science instruction. Psychological Science, 15(10), 661-667.

learning_science.principle: Open-ended investigation and product creation demonstrate creative-productive giftedness (Renzulli Type III)
learning_science.why: Self-directed inquiry with an authentic product captures applied, real-world ability that reasoning batteries structurally omit
learning_science.concrete_decision: Persist the investigation record and conclusion as an artifact and score it with an anchored rubric (M-RUBRIC) for depth and originality of reasoning
learning_science.source: Renzulli, J. S., & Reis, S. M. (2014). The Schoolwide Enrichment Model: A How-to Guide for Talent Development (3rd ed.). Waco, TX: Prufrock Press.

tail_precision_rationale: Keyed items score whether a child knows an answer; they cannot see how a child finds one. M-HYP (informativeness of tests - do successive trials isolate one variable and disambiguate hypotheses?) and M-EXPLORE (breadth of the space investigated) capture scientific-reasoning process; M-PATH records the full test sequence; M-PROG turns the investigation into a curve showing whether the child converges efficiently or flails; and M-RUBRIC with M-POLY grade the reasoning in the recorded conclusion polytomously, extracting tail information from a single rich task. This process-and-product suite is entirely different from the build-and-reflect Maker's Workshop, and at the gifted tail it separates children who investigate strategically from those who test randomly - a demonstrated-achievement axis reasoning cutoffs miss.
age_rationale: Designing a test, holding a variable constant, and interpreting an outcome depend on emerging means-ends and comparative reasoning that are unreliable in kindergarten, so K-1 is served by exploration and creativity types; from about grade 2 upward children can run and interpret simple one-variable investigations, with picture-menu conclusions for 2-3 and short written reasoning for 6-8.

adaptive.content_range: one-variable investigations with an obvious outcome (young) up to multi-variable systems requiring controlled comparison and trade-offs (older)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: number of manipulable variables, noise in the outcome, whether the best answer requires controlling confounds, depth of the required conclusion
adaptive.notes: Partly accuracy-adaptive: escalate the number of interacting variables and outcome subtlety for children who run efficient controlled tests, so the ceiling of investigative reasoning is probed; scoring blends a rubric with process metrics rather than a pure theta.

engagement_hook: A be-a-real-scientist bench where the child freely tinkers, launches trials, and watches results measured live - the satisfying loop of predict, test, and discover drives the task.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Prior hands-on science exposure is a familiarity confound (use novel, self-teaching apparatus and a warm-up); reading load must stay low for young children (voice prompts, picture-menu conclusions); rubric scoring of reasoning has reliability limits (use anchored rubrics, multiple raters, report agreement); fine-motor/device skill can hamper setup (large controls, forgiving inputs); a child may stumble on the answer without reasoning (weight process metrics M-HYP/M-PATH alongside the outcome). Reading policy (D-017): reading is a REQUIRED baseline-literacy capability, not a construct-irrelevant risk to mitigate — instructions and stimuli are on-screen text only (never audio); K-1 uses very simple, high-frequency words a beginning reader can interpret; a child who cannot read the grade-appropriate text is intentionally screened out (capability-to-benefit from reading-based Timeback).

name: Check It Twice
topics_techniques_covered: conscientiousness
one_liner: A robot sorted things in a hurry with a few mistakes; the child may turn it in right away or review and fix it first - whether they check is the measure.
interaction: Items are pre-sorted into two baskets with two planted errors. Each item has a 'check' (mark reviewed) control and a 'move' (switch basket) control, and a big 'turn it in' button is available from the first moment. On submit the engine logs review time, review coverage, corrections, planted errors caught vs missed, and final accuracy. Several rounds test whether checking persists.
self_teach: Wordless demo: a ghost hand inspects an item, moves a misplaced one (it turns green), then presses 'turn it in'; one unscored practice round. Behavior is free - the demo simply shows both options exist.

learning_science.why: Observed self-discipline/carefulness predicts achievement better than Likert self-ratings and resists faking.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Measure whether the child reviews and corrects before submitting, not a questionnaire; always leave an immediate-submit option so checking is voluntary.
learning_science.source: Duckworth, A. & Seligman, M. (2005). Self-discipline outdoes IQ in predicting academic performance of adolescents. Psychological Science.

learning_science.why: Voluntary error-checking is a monitoring-then-control act; catching planted errors indexes calibrated self-monitoring.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Plant known errors and score caught-vs-missed plus review coverage as the monitoring signal.
learning_science.source: Nelson, T. & Narens, L. (1990). Metamemory: a theoretical framework and new findings. Psychology of Learning and Motivation.

learning_science.principle: Validity caveat - separate carefulness from slow processing
learning_science.why: Long review time alone is ambiguous.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Interpret review time jointly with coverage, corrections, and final accuracy; log engagement/idle to exclude disengaged dawdling.
learning_science.source: MacCann, C., Duckworth, A. & Roberts, R. (2009). Empirical identification of the major facets of conscientiousness. Learning and Individual Differences.

tail_precision_rationale: Task commitment/conscientiousness is a construct reasoning tests miss; voluntary review time (M-PERSIST) and coverage (M-PATH), combined with the planted-error catch rate (M-ERRTYPE) and corrections (M-REV), yield a behavioral carefulness index that adds non-cognitive tail signal near the cut. Reading these jointly with final accuracy (M-ACC) and engagement (M-ENGAGE), plus drift across rounds (M-DRIFT), distinguishes durable conscientiousness from a one-off check or from mere slow processing.
age_rationale: Sorting fruit vs veggies with picture items and tap controls suits pre-readers (K-1); content difficulty and item count scale up for older bands. The behavioral signal (does the child check?) is age-general. (D-017: audio is not used — deliver as simple on-screen text; reading is required.)

adaptive.content_range: picture sorts (fruit/veggie, animal habitats) up to more items and subtler category errors
adaptive.difficulty_levers: number of items; number/subtlety of planted errors; optional time-pressure framing
adaptive.notes: Any keyed sort with plantable errors clones this; the measured trait is the checking behavior, so content is a swappable shell.

engagement_hook: Be the one who catches the robot's silly mistakes before they go out - a satisfying 'gotcha' when you spot a slip.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Confounding carefulness with slow processing (read time with coverage/accuracy; log idle/engagement); reading (picture items, tap controls); ensure planted errors are unambiguous so catches are real; do NOT reward submit-speed - the signal is voluntary review, reported behaviorally with an explicit validity caveat. Reading policy (D-017): reading is a REQUIRED baseline-literacy capability, not a construct-irrelevant risk to mitigate — instructions and stimuli are on-screen text only (never audio); K-1 uses very simple, high-frequency words a beginning reader can interpret; a child who cannot read the grade-appropriate text is intentionally screened out (capability-to-benefit from reading-based Timeback).

name: Brainstorm Blaster
topics_techniques_covered: divergent_thinking
alternative uses task
instances task
similarities task
complementary:creativity
one_liner: The child rattles off as many different uses for a common object (or as many things in a category) as they can, and each idea pops onto the screen as a bubble.
interaction: Older children type each idea and press enter; younger children tap picture-icons from a large palette or draw, adding one idea at a time. Every submitted idea becomes a floating bubble; a soft timer runs. The engine logs idea count, timestamps between ideas, and clusters ideas into semantic categories to score fluency, flexibility, originality, and elaboration. No idea is ever marked wrong.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand demo (<=10s) shows a shoe, then a hand adding bubbles: shoe as a hammer, a boat for a mouse, a flower pot - three visibly different ideas floating up, cueing 'many different answers.' One unscored warm-up prompt ('uses for a spoon') lets the child add two ideas before scoring.

learning_science.principle: Divergent production (fluency, flexibility, originality, elaboration) is a distinct component of intellect not captured by convergent reasoning tests
learning_science.why: CogAT-style items have one correct answer and cannot observe idea generation, so the creativity ring of giftedness is unmeasured
learning_science.concrete_decision: Score four separate divergent indices (M-IDEAFLU, M-FLEX, M-ORIG, M-ELAB) from an open Alternative-Uses prompt instead of a single-key item
learning_science.source: Guilford, J. P. (1967). The Nature of Human Intelligence. New York: McGraw-Hill.

learning_science.principle: Creativity is a defining ring of giftedness alongside ability and task commitment
learning_science.why: A defensible gifted identification must sample creative potential, which reasoning batteries structurally miss
learning_science.concrete_decision: Include an open ideation type whose originality score (statistical infrequency vs a norm bank) feeds the creativity ring
learning_science.source: Renzulli, J. S. (1978). What makes giftedness? Reexamining a definition. Phi Delta Kappan, 60(3), 180-184.

learning_science.principle: Originality and flexibility are less coachable and more diagnostic than raw fluency alone
learning_science.why: Fluency inflates with speed/coaching, while switching categories and producing rare-but-appropriate ideas better marks genuine divergent ability
learning_science.concrete_decision: Weight category switches (M-FLEX) and infrequency (M-ORIG) separately so a child cannot win by listing many near-identical ideas
learning_science.source: Runco, M. A., & Acar, S. (2012). Divergent thinking as an indicator of creative potential. Creativity Research Journal, 24(1), 66-75.

new_measurements_proposed.name: Idea fluency
new_measurements_proposed.usefulness_tail: Count of distinct valid ideas in an open divergent task; fluency is the most reliable single divergent-thinking index and higher-ability children generate more, providing a continuous creativity axis CogAT lacks.
new_measurements_proposed.how_to_collect: Count non-duplicate on-topic responses per prompt (dedupe near-identical entries).
new_measurements_proposed.how_much_to_collect: >=3 prompts, roughly 2-3 minutes each, to stabilize the fluency estimate.

new_measurements_proposed.name: Category flexibility
new_measurements_proposed.usefulness_tail: Number of distinct semantic/functional categories the child moves among; flexibility separates truly divergent thinkers from fluent-but-repetitive ones and is harder to coach than raw count.
new_measurements_proposed.how_to_collect: Cluster responses into categories (functional, physical, imaginative) and count distinct categories and switches.
new_measurements_proposed.how_much_to_collect: Same open prompts as fluency; needs a category scheme or embedding model.

new_measurements_proposed.name: Statistical originality
new_measurements_proposed.usefulness_tail: Infrequency of a response against a reference norm bank; rare-but-appropriate ideas are the cleanest creativity tail signal and mark the Renzulli creativity ring.
new_measurements_proposed.how_to_collect: Score each response's frequency against a norm corpus; low frequency plus on-topic appropriateness scores as original.
new_measurements_proposed.how_much_to_collect: Requires a norm bank per prompt; >=3 prompts per child.

new_measurements_proposed.name: Elaboration
new_measurements_proposed.usefulness_tail: Amount of detail/embellishment added to an idea or figure (extra words, sub-features, strokes); adds incremental creativity variance beyond how many ideas are produced.
new_measurements_proposed.how_to_collect: Count added descriptors/words per verbal idea or strokes/added features per figural response.
new_measurements_proposed.how_much_to_collect: Open verbal and figural tasks; interpret relative to time on task.

tail_precision_rationale: A reasoning cutoff cannot see idea generation at all. Fluency (M-IDEAFLU) gives a continuous ideation axis, but at the gifted tail M-FLEX (category switching) and M-ORIG (statistical infrequency vs norms) are the sharp separators: two children who list ten uses differ enormously if one stays in a single category and the other spans functional, physical, and imaginative frames with rare ideas. M-ELAB adds detail variance, and M-PERSIST (ideas produced in the final third of the window) distinguishes children who keep generating after the obvious ideas are exhausted - a task-commitment x creativity interaction invisible to CogAT.
age_rationale: Presentation adapts to literacy: K-1 and early 2-3 use picture-icon tapping or drawing (picture-prompted alternate uses, no typing), while 4-5 and 6-8 type free-text ideas. The core generate-many-answers demand is developmentally appropriate from kindergarten upward.

adaptive.content_range: concrete familiar objects (shoe, cup) for young children up to abstract prompts (uses for the number zero, ways two ideas are alike) for older
adaptive.difficulty_levers: object abstractness, category constraints ('only imaginative uses'), time window length, prompt novelty
adaptive.notes: Not a classic-CAT construct: there is no single difficulty ladder, so 'adaptivity' means selecting prompts of varying abstractness and constraint and adjusting the time window; branching is on prompt type, not on right/wrong.

engagement_hook: Ideas literally blast onto the screen as colorful floating bubbles with a combo meter that rewards switching to a new kind of idea, turning brainstorming into a rapid-fire game.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Verbal fluency and vocabulary can confound verbal ideation (offer picture/drawing modes to reduce the language load); typing speed can penalize older children (allow voice-to-text or picture modes); automated originality scoring has low reliability and can misjudge child-appropriate ideas (use norm banks and human/expert audit); avoid rewarding sheer speed at the expense of appropriateness. Reading policy (D-017): reading is a REQUIRED baseline-literacy capability, not a construct-irrelevant risk to mitigate — instructions and stimuli are on-screen text only (never audio); K-1 uses very simple, high-frequency words a beginning reader can interpret; a child who cannot read the grade-appropriate text is intentionally screened out (capability-to-benefit from reading-based Timeback).

name: Squiggle Studio
topics_techniques_covered: figural_creativity
line meanings
picture completion
pattern meanings
complementary:creativity
one_liner: The child is shown an abstract squiggle or half-finished shape and turns it into as many different pictures as they can by drawing on top of it.
interaction: A starter squiggle appears on a canvas. The child draws with a finger/mouse to complete it into a recognizable thing, taps 'New idea' to get a fresh copy of the same squiggle and make something different, and can label each creation from a picture menu or text. The engine logs number of distinct interpretations, stroke counts (elaboration), drawing time, and reuse-vs-transform of the base line. Nothing is graded right or wrong.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand demo (<=10s) shows one squiggle becoming a snake, then the same squiggle (fresh copy) becoming a smile on a face, then a mountain - three different pictures from the identical line, cueing 'make it into something, then something else.' One unscored warm-up squiggle lets the child draw once before scoring.

learning_science.principle: Figural divergent thinking (picture construction/completion) captures creative potential with minimal language load
learning_science.why: Verbal creativity tasks confound creativity with vocabulary; figural tasks let non-verbal and multilingual children show originality
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use an open figural-completion canvas scored for fluency, originality, and elaboration to broaden who can demonstrate creativity (H4)
learning_science.source: Torrance, E. P. (1974). Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking: Norms-Technical Manual. Bensenville, IL: Scholastic Testing Service.

learning_science.principle: Elaboration - adding detail and transforming a given stimulus - is a core figural-creativity index
learning_science.why: How much a child develops and reinterprets a base figure distinguishes surface from deep creative processing
learning_science.concrete_decision: Log stroke counts and base-line transformation (M-ELAB, M-PATH) as separate scores from the number of interpretations
learning_science.source: Torrance, E. P. (1966/1974). Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking (figural forms), scored on fluency, originality, elaboration, abstractness, and resistance to premature closure.

learning_science.principle: Creativity products are best judged by appropriateness plus novelty, ideally via consensual/expert rating
learning_science.why: Automated creativity scoring is unreliable, so figural products should support later human consensual assessment
learning_science.concrete_decision: Store each drawing as a reviewable artifact so a Consensual Assessment Technique panel can rate originality, not just the automated counts
learning_science.source: Amabile, T. M. (1982). Social psychology of creativity: A consensual assessment technique. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 43(5), 997-1013.

tail_precision_rationale: CogAT figural items ask the child to pick a completion, never to produce one, so creative production is unobserved. Here M-IDEAFLU (distinct interpretations of one squiggle) and M-ORIG (how rare each interpretation is) provide a production-based creativity axis; M-ELAB (stroke count, added features) and M-PATH (how radically the base line is transformed vs merely traced) separate children who reinterpret the stimulus from those who add token detail. M-PERSIST (still generating new pictures late in the window) captures the resistance-to-premature-closure that marks gifted figural creativity and is invisible to a multiple-choice cutoff.
age_rationale: Finger/mouse drawing is accessible from kindergarten; the task needs no reading and labels come from a picture menu for pre-readers. Older children produce more elaborated and abstract interpretations, but the same canvas mechanic works across all bands with only fidelity of drawing differing.

adaptive.content_range: simple single squiggles or half-shapes (young) up to ambiguous multi-line stimuli and 'make it abstract' constraints (older)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: stimulus ambiguity, number of base lines, constraints ('make something that moves'), time window
adaptive.notes: Open production task, not accuracy-adaptive: procedurally generate squiggles of graded ambiguity and vary constraints; branching selects stimulus complexity rather than scoring correctness.

engagement_hook: A playful art-studio canvas where the same doodle magically resets so kids can 'see how many things hide in one squiggle' - open-ended drawing feels like free play, not a test.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Fine-motor and device-drawing skill can confound figural output (score interpretation count and transformation, not draw quality; allow stamps for very young children); automated originality of drawings is unreliable (retain artifacts for consensual expert rating and flag low scoring reliability); touch vs mouse hardware differences add noise (normalize by device). Reading policy (D-017): reading is a REQUIRED baseline-literacy capability, not a construct-irrelevant risk to mitigate — instructions and stimuli are on-screen text only (never audio); K-1 uses very simple, high-frequency words a beginning reader can interpret; a child who cannot read the grade-appropriate text is intentionally screened out (capability-to-benefit from reading-based Timeback).

name: Shape Morph
topics_techniques_covered: figure_analogy: A is to B as C is to ? using geometric shapes; infer the A-to-B transformation and apply it to C (NNAT format)
figure_analogy: two figures related by a rule, then a third with options; pick the figure completing the analogy (ICAR figural analogies)
figure_analogy: simple A:B::C:? with one clear change (e.g. big to small)
figure_analogy: A:B::C:? with two shapes changing by one combined rule (size and shade)
one_liner: A first shape turns into a second; the child makes the third shape change the same way by picking the matching fourth.
interaction: The top row shows A with an animated morph arrow into B. The bottom row shows C, an arrow, and an empty slot with 4 options below. The child taps the option that is to C what B is to A; it snaps into the slot. An optional two-icon confidence tap (a star for sure, a wavy hand for not sure) appears, then GO submits.
self_teach: The ghost-hand replays the A-to-B morph (e.g., big shrinks to small), then applies the same shrink to C and taps the matching option; the analogy row lights up. Warm-up: big circle to small circle, so big square to ? (small square).

learning_science.why: Analogical reasoning requires mapping the relation, not the surface, from base to target.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Distractors include a literal copy of C and a wrong-transform foil so only relational mapping, not surface matching, is credited.
learning_science.source: Gentner (1983), Cognitive Science 7(2)

learning_science.why: Children move from surface to relational responding as knowledge and working memory grow, setting a floor age for abstract figural analogy.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Bands start at grades 2-3 with a single obvious change and add a second combined rule by 6-8, matching the relational shift.
learning_science.source: Rattermann & Gentner (1998), in Piaget, Evolution, and Development

learning_science.why: Confidence accuracy adds incremental validity and down-weights lucky guesses at the tail.
learning_science.concrete_decision: A quick optional two-level confidence tap is collected on a subset so calibration can be modeled without burden.
learning_science.source: Fleming & Lau (2014), Frontiers in Human Neuroscience 8:443

tail_precision_rationale: M-ERRTYPE uses a designed distractor set - a literal-copy foil (no transform applied), a wrong-attribute foil, and an over/under-application foil - so a wrong answer reveals exactly where the relational mapping broke and grades how far below the analogy cut a child sits. On two-rule items the same distractor keying feeds the proposed M-RULEID (how many transformations were correctly applied), separating one-rule from two-rule mappers at the tail. M-RTFIRST captures the map-before-act latency typical of strong reasoners, and M-CONF on a subset removes lucky guesses via confidence-accuracy calibration.
age_rationale: Figural analogy requires holding an abstract transformation and re-applying it. With familiar relations this appears early, but reliable mapping over arbitrary figural transforms is not dependable until roughly grades 2-3 (ages 7-9); K-1 is excluded because at ages 5-6 such mapping is unstable and would measure developmental stage rather than reasoning (Goswami 1992; Rattermann & Gentner 1998). 2-3 uses one salient change; 4-5 a clear single transform with confusable foils; 6-8 combines two transforms. Big tap options keep motor demands low.

adaptive.content_range: single obvious transform A:B::C:? (grades 2-3) up to two combined transforms with relational distractors (6-8)
difficulty_levers: number of transformations 1 to 2+
transformation type: size, rotation, fill/shade, count, reflection, add/delete element
abstractness of shapes
distractor design: literal-copy, wrong-attribute, over-application foils
option count
adaptive.notes: A:B::C:? items generate from a transform grammar with relationally-keyed distractors; unlimited clones and clean difficulty control via transform count.

engagement_hook: A magic morph - watching A visibly transform into B and then casting the same spell on C is playful and makes the hidden rule tangible.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Exclude K-1 to avoid measuring the relational shift instead of reasoning; include a literal-copy foil so surface matching does not score; pair shade/color with shape; keep the confidence tap optional and non-punitive; big tap options remove motor load; the ghost-hand morph plus warm-up controls novelty. Reading policy (D-017): reading is a REQUIRED baseline-literacy capability, not a construct-irrelevant risk to mitigate — instructions and stimuli are on-screen text only (never audio); K-1 uses very simple, high-frequency words a beginning reader can interpret; a child who cannot read the grade-appropriate text is intentionally screened out (capability-to-benefit from reading-based Timeback).

name: Pattern Carpet
topics_techniques_covered: figure_series: a sequence of figures changes by a consistent rule across the row; pick the figure that continues the sequence (NNAT/CFIT serial-reasoning format)
figure_series: a row of figures follows a progression on one or more attributes (size up, fixed-step rotation, increasing count); pick the next figure
figure_series: a simple repeating or growing picture pattern (AB AB, or +1 dot each step)
figural_matrix: 3x3 array where each row AND each column is a progression and the bottom-right cell continues both (progression-rule matrix)
matrix_induction: derive the missing cell of a progression grid from the row and column progressions
figural_matrix: cognitive-model-driven difficulty across the full K-8 range
one_liner: The child continues a woven pattern by picking the tile that keeps every row (and column) progressing the same way.
interaction: A single row (simplest) or a 3x3 carpet is shown where each row is a progression on one or more attributes; the last cell is empty with 4 candidate tiles below. The child taps the tile that continues the row's progression (and, in grid mode, the column's progression too); it snaps into the slot (tap another to swap), then taps GO. No typing, no reading.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand sweeps left-to-right along a row with a rhythmic pulse on each figure (implying the growing step), then taps the tray tile that continues the weave; the carpet completes and its pattern animates. One unscored +1-dot single-row warm-up runs before scoring begins.

learning_science.principle: Fluid intelligence via inductive rule extraction
learning_science.why: Continuing a figural progression taps culture-fair Gf by requiring rule induction from a serial change.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Rows are built from attribute progressions (size, count, rotation) so the task loads inductive reasoning rather than crystallized knowledge or notation.
learning_science.source: Cattell (1963), Journal of Educational Psychology 54(1)

learning_science.why: Item difficulty rises with the number of elements and simultaneous progression rules that must be tracked.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Difficulty escalates by adding parallel progressions (more attributes, plus the column axis in grid mode) rather than surface clutter, so the ceiling probes how many progressions a child tracks at once.
learning_science.source: Primi (2001), Intelligence 30(1)

learning_science.why: Matched clones at the same difficulty reduce the conditional standard error of a tail decision.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Each scored item ships with an AIG-cloned twin at the same progression set so response consistency can be logged.
learning_science.source: Embretson & Reise (2000), Item Response Theory for Psychologists

tail_precision_rationale: M-DIFFREACH under adaptive escalation of the number of simultaneous progressions (single-attribute row up to a 3x3 with row and column progressions on two attributes) walks each child to the exact number of parallel progressions they can track. M-ERRTYPE distinguishes an off-by-one step (near-miss) or a previous-term periodicity slip from a random pick, refining where below the cut a child sits. M-CONSIST on an equal-difficulty twin shrinks the conditional standard error near the cut, and M-RTFIRST with M-RT credit reflective extraction of a multi-attribute progression over fast single-attribute pattern-matching.
age_rationale: Continuing a short repeating or +1 growing pattern is accessible to K-1 in single-row mode (big tap targets, no reading). 2-3 adds a single-attribute progression; 4-5 combines two attributes; 6-8 uses the 3x3 grid where row and column progressions must both hold with fixed-step rotation plus count. The K-8 tag reflects the shell spanning the full progressive-matrix difficulty range as one cognitive-model-driven bank (matching GF-006/GF-009 and, in single-row mode, GF-018). Continuation is developmentally accessible early, so the shell spans all bands.

adaptive.content_range: AB-AB and +1 single-row patterns (K-1) up to a 3x3 carpet with two-attribute row and column progressions and fixed-step rotation (6-8)
difficulty_levers: single row vs 3x3 grid (add the column axis)
number of attributes progressing 1 to 3
step size and whether the step is constant or accelerating
distractor closeness: off-by-one step, previous term, wrong attribute
sequence/grid length
adaptive.notes: A progression grammar generates rows (and columns) and unlimited parallel forms; twin clones at equal difficulty enable consistency and drift checks; single-row items and full grids come from the same generator.

engagement_hook: Weaving a carpet that keeps growing - snapping the tile that continues the pattern triggers a satisfying continue-the-weave animation across the whole grid.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Avoid reading and numerals (use dots/shapes, not written numbers, for count); large tap options remove motor demands; key distractors to specific progression errors to block surface guessing; pair color with shape; keep pacing self-directed so processing speed does not contaminate the reasoning score; ghost-hand plus warm-up controls novelty. Reading policy (D-017): reading is a REQUIRED baseline-literacy capability, not a construct-irrelevant risk to mitigate — instructions and stimuli are on-screen text only (never audio); K-1 uses very simple, high-frequency words a beginning reader can interpret; a child who cannot read the grade-appropriate text is intentionally screened out (capability-to-benefit from reading-based Timeback).

name: Mystery Gate
topics_techniques_covered: visual_rule_discovery: a hidden gate accepts only figures obeying a secret rule; the child DESIGNS their own test figures, feeds them in, and reads accept/reject feedback to induce the rule (active/selection concept learning rather than sorting a given queue)
visual_rule_discovery: two sets of figures - those the gate accepts vs rejects - implicitly define the criterial feature the child must isolate
inductive_reasoning: infer a general rule from self-generated positive and negative evidence, then apply it to classify new probe figures
figure_classification: after the rule is found, decide for each probe figure whether it belongs (obeys the rule) or not
nonverbal_deduction: full content-range coverage across this type's difficulty spectrum (recat full-range retag)
one_liner: A magic gate opens only for figures that follow a secret rule; the child builds their own figures to test, watches which pass, then uses what they learned to judge new figures.
interaction: The child assembles a test figure from a small feature palette (tap to set shape, color, and count), then taps SEND to push it through the gate; the gate glows and opens (accept) or buzzes and bounces it back (reject), and the figure drops into an ACCEPTED or REJECTED tray. The child runs as many self-chosen tests as they like. When ready they tap I KNOW IT, and three probe figures appear one at a time; for each the child taps the OPEN gate (belongs) or the CLOSED gate (does not) to classify it. A hint lamp reveals one extra accepted example. Only the three final classifications are scored; the tests are the process record.
self_teach: The ghost-hand builds one figure on the palette (two taps), sends it, and the gate opens with a green glow and the figure lands in the ACCEPTED tray; it then builds a second figure that the gate buzzes and bounces into the REJECTED tray, making accept/reject obvious wordlessly. The warm-up uses a blatant one-color rule so the child feels the test-then-learn loop once before scoring.

learning_science.why: Letting the learner choose which cases to test is a distinct, more diagnostic paradigm than classifying a supplied sequence; selection strategies reveal how systematically a child isolates a variable.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The child constructs and selects each test figure themselves rather than sorting a fixed queue, so the action log captures experimental strategy, not just classification accuracy.
learning_science.source: Bruner, Goodnow & Austin (1956), A Study of Thinking

learning_science.principle: Hypothesis space search / scientific discovery as dual search
learning_science.why: Rule discovery is a search over hypotheses guided by chosen experiments; efficient searchers run maximally informative tests.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Difficulty is set by how large the hypothesis space is (features that vary), and M-HYP scores whether the child's chosen tests are disambiguating (vary one feature) or redundant.
learning_science.source: Klahr & Dunbar (1988), Cognitive Science 12(1)

learning_science.why: Even young children can select evidence that reduces uncertainty; the quality of self-directed sampling is a strong reasoning signal.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The design rewards controlled, one-variable-at-a-time tests over confounded ones, surfacing the control-of-variables strategy without instruction.
learning_science.source: Schulz & Bonawitz (2007), Developmental Psychology 43(4)

tail_precision_rationale: Because the child designs their own experiments, M-HYP (informativeness of each self-chosen test) and M-EFF (tests used vs the minimum needed to disambiguate) isolate strategic inductive reasoners far more sharply than final accuracy: two children can both classify the probes correctly yet differ by running 3 controlled tests vs 12 confounded ones. M-PROG turns the test stream into an uncertainty-reduction curve (a dynamic-assessment learning-rate signal), M-PATH records the exact experiment sequence for evidence-model scoring, and hint-free discovery (M-HINT) is stronger evidence at the ceiling.
age_rationale: Designing and revising experiments demands generating hypotheses and holding a variable constant, which the 2026-07 review judged out of reach below 4-5 (K-1 and 2-3 are served by the simpler FLU classification and series types). The bank therefore starts at the 4-5 rung (difficulty 8 on the 1-20 scale) and generates nothing below it. 4-5 uses a single-attribute rule with more distractor dimensions; 6-8 uses conjunctive rules over two attributes and can delay feedback until SEND batches. Tap-to-build with large targets keeps motor load low.

adaptive.content_range: single obvious-feature gate with a tiny feature palette (grades 2-3) up to conjunctive/relational hidden rules over many varying dimensions (6-8)
difficulty_levers: size of the hypothesis space (number of features that vary)
rule form: single feature to conjunction to relational
salience of the criterial feature
feedback immediacy (per-send vs batched)
number of allowed tests before I KNOW IT
adaptive.notes: Rules and feature palettes are procedurally sampled; an automated uniqueness/identifiability check confirms the accept-set determines exactly one intended rule, so items clone at high throughput once audited.

engagement_hook: You are a scientist running experiments on a magic gate - every figure you invent is a little test, and the thrill of cracking the secret rule with a clever probe is intrinsically rewarding.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Audit that the accept-set uniquely identifies the rule so M-HYP is meaningful; cap or de-emphasize test count so trial-and-error flooding is not rewarded (M-EFF penalizes it); pair color with shape/count so color-blind children are not disadvantaged; keep hints non-punitive but logged; ghost-hand plus warm-up controls novelty; exclude K-1 to avoid a floor that would misread as low ability. Reading policy (D-017): reading is a REQUIRED baseline-literacy capability, not a construct-irrelevant risk to mitigate — instructions and stimuli are on-screen text only (never audio); K-1 uses very simple, high-frequency words a beginning reader can interpret; a child who cannot read the grade-appropriate text is intentionally screened out (capability-to-benefit from reading-based Timeback).

name: Clue Detective
topics_techniques_covered: nonverbal_deduction: clue cards each state a pictorial constraint (has a hole, not blue, three sides); the child eliminates every figure that violates each clue until one survivor remains

nonverbal_deduction: choose the figure where a spatial/attribute condition holds (a dot inside the circle but outside the square; the star above the box AND inside the ring) by accumulating constraints
nonverbal_deduction: deduce which figure is forced once all constraints are applied (constraint satisfaction by elimination rather than Latin-square uniqueness)
figure_classification: interpret each clue as a positive/negative property test applied to a lineup of candidates
one_liner: A lineup of figures hides one culprit; clue cards flip over one at a time and the child crosses out every figure a clue rules out until only the answer is left.
interaction: Six candidate figures sit in a lineup. Clue cards (wordless icons, e.g., a crossed-out blue swatch = not blue; a hole icon = must have a hole) reveal one at a time. After each clue the child taps the figures it eliminates (they dim and get an X); a mis-eliminated figure can be tapped again to restore it. When the child believes one figure survives all clues, they tap it in a final SELECT slot to answer. Eliminations are process-scored; the final pick is the keyed answer.
self_teach: The ghost-hand reveals the first clue card, then taps the two figures that clash with it - each dims with an X - and shakes its head at a figure that fits (leaving it lit). The warm-up runs a two-clue puzzle with obvious color/shape clues so the eliminate-the-violators loop is felt once before scoring.

learning_science.principle: Deductive constraint satisfaction / process of elimination
learning_science.why: Narrowing a candidate set by successively applying constraints is prototypical deductive reasoning distinct from inductive pattern completion.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Each clue is a logical filter; the answer is the unique figure consistent with the conjunction of all clues, and the child must apply negation and conjunction correctly.
learning_science.source: Johnson-Laird (1983), Mental Models

learning_science.why: Efficient reasoners eliminate as soon as a clue falsifies a candidate rather than re-checking everything, showing model-based deduction.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The elimination log shows whether the child prunes decisively per clue (efficient) or thrashes, and M-EFF compares eliminations to the minimum forced by each clue.
learning_science.source: Markovits & Barrouillet (2002), Developmental Review 22(1)

learning_science.principle: Cognitive load managed by externalizing state
learning_science.why: Letting the child mark eliminations offloads working memory so the measured construct is deduction, not memory span.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Crossed-out figures stay visibly dimmed so the child reasons over the shrinking set without holding it in mind.
learning_science.source: Sweller (1988), Cognitive Science 12(2)

tail_precision_rationale: M-POLY awards graded credit for the fraction of clues correctly applied even when the final pick is wrong, extracting tail information from one rich deduction puzzle (a single item behaves like several). M-EFF measures whether each elimination is exactly forced by the current clue (no over- or under-pruning), separating decisive deductive reasoners from guess-and-check, and M-PATH records the clue-by-clue elimination order for evidence-model scoring. M-ERRTYPE tags whether errors come from mishandling negation (not-blue) vs conjunction, and M-REV flags confident, targeted revisions vs thrashing.
age_rationale: Applying negation and conjunction across accumulating constraints is unreliable in K-1 (served by positive-match classification types). 2-3 uses two positive single-feature clues over four candidates; 4-5 introduces negation (not-blue) and three clues over six candidates; 6-8 uses conjunctive and relational spatial clues. Large tap targets and persistent dimming keep motor and memory load low.

adaptive.content_range: two positive single-feature clues over four candidates (grades 2-3) up to conjunctive and relational spatial clues over six-plus candidates (6-8)
difficulty_levers: number of clues and candidates
clue polarity (positive vs negated) and logical form (single vs conjunctive)
relational/spatial clues (inside, above) vs simple attribute clues
how much each clue prunes (forcing more inference per step)
perceptual similarity among candidates
adaptive.notes: Candidate lineups and clue sets are generated so the conjunction yields exactly one survivor; an automated solver verifies uniqueness and minimum-elimination counts, enabling high-throughput cloning.

engagement_hook: A whodunit: each flipped clue card lets you rule out suspects, and the detective satisfaction of narrowing six figures down to the one culprit keeps kids leaning in.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Verify the clue conjunction yields a unique survivor and that clue icons are unambiguous (no reading) so the format is language-neutral; make elimination reversible so a mis-tap is not scored as reasoning error; pair color clues with shape/pattern clues; persistent dimming offloads memory so working memory is not confounded; ghost-hand plus warm-up controls the novel elimination mechanic. Reading policy (D-017): reading is a REQUIRED baseline-literacy capability, not a construct-irrelevant risk to mitigate — instructions and stimuli are on-screen text only (never audio); K-1 uses very simple, high-frequency words a beginning reader can interpret; a child who cannot read the grade-appropriate text is intentionally screened out (capability-to-benefit from reading-based Timeback).

name: Copy the Change
topics_techniques_covered: visual_rule_discovery: a few input-to-output grid examples demonstrate a transformation rule; infer the rule and construct the output grid for a new input
visual_rule_discovery: one worked example shows a small grid changing (e.g. all shapes shift right); apply the same change to a new grid by tapping cells
one_liner: A small example shows a grid changing; the child makes the same change happen on a new grid by tapping cells.
interaction: The top shows a worked example as an animated before-to-after grid pair. Below sit a new before grid and an editable after grid (initialized as a copy of the new before). The child taps cells to change them (a tap cycles a cell through the available colors/states; tap-and-hold clears) to produce the transformed output, then taps GO. Snap-to-cell tapping; no reading.
self_teach: The ghost-hand plays the example transform (e.g., every filled cell slides one column right) as an animation, then on the new grid taps the cells to reproduce the same slide; the output glows when it matches. Warm-up: a one-row 1x3 shift.

learning_science.principle: Abstraction and reasoning from few examples
learning_science.why: Inferring a transformation from one or few input-output pairs and applying it to a new case is a hallmark of fluid intelligence.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Items give one or few worked transforms and require constructing (not selecting) the output, following the ARC abstraction-and-reasoning paradigm.
learning_science.source: Chollet (2019), On the Measure of Intelligence, arXiv:1911.01547

learning_science.why: A studied example plus a completion problem builds a transferable schema at lower load than open problem solving.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The child studies the animated example, then completes the analogous output - a completion-problem design.
learning_science.source: Renkl & Atkinson (2003), Educational Psychologist 38(1)

learning_science.why: Building an output rather than picking one yields per-cell graded evidence and blocks lucky guessing.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The output is scored per cell (polytomous) so near-correct constructions earn graded credit.
learning_science.source: Embretson & Reise (2000), Item Response Theory for Psychologists

tail_precision_rationale: Because the child constructs the output, M-POLY scores per-cell correctness so a near-correct grid (right rule, one slip) earns graded credit and places the child precisely where free selection cannot. M-PATH with M-EFF compare the child's edit sequence to the minimal set of changes: constructing exactly the needed cells (no flailing) at a multi-rule transform is a strong ceiling separator and feeds the proposed M-HYP for how systematically the rule was applied. M-REV and M-PROG show whether the child locked the rule immediately or converged by trial-and-error. Guessing is near-impossible for a constructed grid, so accuracy at high difficulty is unusually clean tail evidence.
age_rationale: Constructing a transformed grid demands inferring a rule and executing multiple coordinated edits. The 2026-07 review opened K-1 on a translation-only, single-colour ladder ("for k-1, focus on translations"), where the whole pattern slides as one piece and only a few cells change; the earlier fine-motor and working-memory objection to K-1 stands for every heavier family and is why the ladder is banded by transform. 2-3 keeps one rule but adds colour; 4-5 introduces rotation; 6-8 combines translation, colour and rotation. Tap-to-cycle cells with large targets keep edits feasible. Reflections and the other families the review did not band are served only in the above-level ceiling rungs (difficulty 16-20), which report as 6-8.

adaptive.content_range: apply a single shown transform on a small grid (grades 2-3) up to infer-and-construct multi-step or conditional transforms on larger grids (6-8, ARC-like tail)
difficulty_levers: transformation complexity: translate to recolor to reflect/rotate to conditional/relational
grid size and number of objects
one worked example vs infer from multiple examples
number of coordinated edits required
whether the examples imply a single vs multiple plausible rules
adaptive.notes: Transforms are program-sampled and applied to random grids to make input-output pairs; needs a check that the shown examples imply a unique transform, so cloning is high-throughput with a uniqueness audit.

engagement_hook: You are the copy-machine wizard - learn a secret change from one example then perform it yourself; building the answer feels like casting the rule rather than picking from a menu.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Ensure the example(s) imply a unique transform so per-cell scoring is fair; large tap-to-cycle cells plus undo reduce motor and slip errors; pair color with pattern; no reading; ghost-hand plus warm-up controls novelty; exclude K-1 due to multi-edit motor and working-memory demands. Reading policy (D-017): reading is a REQUIRED baseline-literacy capability, not a construct-irrelevant risk to mitigate — instructions and stimuli are on-screen text only (never audio); K-1 uses very simple, high-frequency words a beginning reader can interpret; a child who cannot read the grade-appropriate text is intentionally screened out (capability-to-benefit from reading-based Timeback).

name: Ranking Ladder
topics_techniques_covered: nonverbal_deduction: integrate a chain of pairwise comparison clues (A beats B, B beats C) to deduce the single forced total order and read off the item forced into a queried rank
nonverbal_deduction: seat each figure in the one position consistent with all given relations, using transitivity to fix positions that no single clue states directly
one_liner: Clue cards each show one thing beating another; the child stacks all the clues together to work out the full winner-to-loser order and seats each character on the right rung.
interaction: A ladder (or podium) with empty rungs stands beside a row of characters and a small stack of clue cards. Each clue card wordlessly shows one character above/beating another (a see-saw tipping, a race arrow, or a taller-than bar). The child taps a card to spotlight the two characters it links, then taps a character and taps a rung to seat it (drag also works); the child may reseat freely until satisfied and taps DONE to commit. Harder items ask only for one queried rung ('who is on the gold rung?') by tapping a character. No numbers, no reading.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand flips two clue cards - one shows a bunny above a frog, the next a frog above a snail - then slides bunny, frog and snail onto the top, middle and bottom rungs in order and the ladder glows; the transitive chain is shown, not told, in under 10s. One unscored warm-up with three characters and two adjacent clues runs before scored items begin.

learning_science.why: The number of relations that must be integrated simultaneously predicts item difficulty and separates children by the relational load they can bind at once - a core fluid-reasoning limit.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Items scale from 2 to 5 chained relations and each distractor rung is keyed so a near-miss violates exactly one relation, exposing how many relations the child integrated.
learning_science.source: Halford, Wilson & Phillips (1998), 'Processing capacity defined by relational complexity', Behavioral and Brain Sciences 21(6):803-831.

learning_science.why: Deducing an unstated ordering (A>C from A>B and B>C) indexes genuine relational reasoning rather than recall, and its development marks reasoning maturity.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Queried ranks are chosen so the answer is fixed only by a non-adjacent, never-directly-stated pair, forcing transitive integration rather than clue lookup.
learning_science.source: Andrews & Halford (2002), 'A cognitive complexity metric applied to cognitive development', Cognitive Psychology 45(2):153-219.

learning_science.principle: Self-teaching via a wordless worked example
learning_science.why: A concrete animated ordering of the chain teaches the novel stacking mechanic without language.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The ghost-hand demo animates building one full order from two clues, plus one unscored warm-up, before scoring.
learning_science.source: Mayer (2005), The Cambridge Handbook of Multimedia Learning. Cambridge University Press.

tail_precision_rationale: M-RULEID (the maximum number of chained relations the child correctly integrates) turns one ordering into a graded relational-complexity signal that a single right/wrong hides, placing children precisely by the relational load they can bind. M-HYP captures whether the child seats the fully-constrained (forced) characters first - an efficient deduction order - versus guessing then reshuffling, and M-ERRTYPE distinguishes an adjacent-swap near-miss (latent ability just below the cut) from a random order. M-RTFIRST marks the reflective planning pause of able integrators, while M-DIFFREACH escalates chain length to find the child's integration ceiling.
age_rationale: Transitive integration of multiple premises is fragile before roughly age 6-7, so K-1 is excluded (served by simpler classification and series types). 2-3 uses short 3-item chains with all-adjacent clues and a visible see-saw so partial ordering is perceptible; 4-5 adds a fourth item and one non-adjacent query; 6-8 uses 5-item chains, redundant or omitted clues, and two-attribute orders (order by height, break ties by width) that demand pure integration. Tap-to-seat with large snap targets keeps motor demand low.

adaptive.content_range: 3-item all-adjacent chains with a perceptible see-saw cue (2-3) up to 5-item chains with non-adjacent queries, redundant or slightly-underdetermined clues, and tie-break second attributes (6-8 tail)
difficulty_levers: number of items in the order (chain length)
number of relations that must be integrated
adjacent vs non-adjacent (transitive) queried pair
redundant vs minimal vs slightly-underdetermined clue sets
single-attribute vs tie-broken two-attribute ordering
presence vs absence of a perceptual magnitude cue on each clue
adaptive.notes: Orders are generated as permutations; a clue subset is sampled and checked for a unique consistent ordering (or a named ambiguity); distractor rungs are derived by single-relation violations for M-ERRTYPE, and the solver computes the optimal seating order for M-HYP.

engagement_hook: Building a champions' podium from scattered match-up cards - each clue snaps two characters into their pecking order and the ladder lights up top-to-bottom when the whole ranking is right, a satisfying tournament-bracket payoff.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Keep clues wordless (see-saw/arrow icons) so it is not a reading test; make relations perceptual for young bands but remove the cue at the tail so success reflects integration not perception; large tap-snap rungs limit fine-motor load; ensure characters differ by shape not colour alone for colour-vision differences; the ghost-hand plus warm-up controls the novel stacking mechanic. Reading policy (D-017): reading is a REQUIRED baseline-literacy capability, not a construct-irrelevant risk to mitigate — instructions and stimuli are on-screen text only (never audio); K-1 uses very simple, high-frequency words a beginning reader can interpret; a child who cannot read the grade-appropriate text is intentionally screened out (capability-to-benefit from reading-based Timeback).

name: Machine Matrix
topics_techniques_covered: figural_matrix: 2x2 and 3x3 matrix completion (missing bottom-right cell)
figural_matrix: Raven-like relational rules running across rows and columns
figural_matrix: abstract colored shapes varying by shape/color/size/position
figural_matrix: RPM rule taxonomy - constant-in-a-row, progression, distribution-of-three, arithmetic add/subtract of a numeric attribute
figural_matrix: logical relations (XOR, OR, AND, consistent union) over attributes (size, color, position, number)
figural_matrix: cognitive-model-driven difficulty (rule count x abstraction x perceptual load)
one_liner: The child taps the one tile that completes a glowing figural matrix so the machine powers on.
interaction: A 2x2 or 3x3 grid is shown with the bottom-right cell empty and 4-6 candidate tiles in a tray below. The child taps a candidate to snap it into the empty cell (tapping another candidate swaps it), then taps the pulsing GO button to submit. One confirmed selection is the answer; no typing, no reading.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand hovers the empty cell, glides to the correct tray tile, taps it (it snaps into the cell), and the machine lights up - under 10s. Then one unscored 2x2 warm-up gives a green pulse for correct or a gentle shake plus the answer for wrong, before scored items begin.

learning_science.principle: Cognitive load theory - minimize extraneous load
learning_science.why: Written rubrics and notation add extraneous load that masks the reasoning being measured.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Zero text; a wordless ghost-hand demo and snap-to-cell tiles carry all instruction so working memory is spent on the relations, not the interface.
learning_science.source: Sweller, van Merrienboer & Paas (1998), Educational Psychology Review 10(3)

learning_science.why: Reasoning difficulty is set by how many relations must be bound simultaneously, the true tail driver in matrices.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Difficulty escalates by adding co-acting rules (1 to 4) rather than surface clutter, so the ceiling probes relational binding capacity.
learning_science.source: Halford, Wilson & Phillips (1998), Behavioral and Brain Sciences 21(6)

learning_science.principle: Process account of the Raven Progressive Matrices
learning_science.why: RPM ability is explained by rule induction and goal management over a fixed rule taxonomy.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Items are generated from the constant/progression/distribution-of-three/arithmetic rule set with distractors keyed to specific rule violations.
learning_science.source: Carpenter, Just & Shell (1990), Psychological Review 97(3)

learning_science.why: A demonstrated solution before independent practice lowers load and speeds schema formation.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The ghost-hand solves one item fully (worked example); the warm-up fades to a hint-only glow; scored items are unguided.
learning_science.source: Renkl & Atkinson (2003), Educational Psychologist 38(1)

new_measurements_proposed.name: Rule dimensionality solved
new_measurements_proposed.what: Number of independent relational rules or attributes the child integrated simultaneously in the correct answer (e.g., a 3x3 matrix solved under three co-acting rules).
new_measurements_proposed.usefulness_tail: Separates children by the relational complexity they can bind at once (Halford). Two children may both be correct, but at 1 vs 3 co-acting rules; exposing that structure sharpens tail placement where a single difficulty index blurs it, and it is harder to coach than surface speed.
new_measurements_proposed.how_to_collect: Tag each item with its rule set and design distractors so each foil violates exactly one named rule; the chosen option reveals which rule-dimensions were satisfied. Log the maximum simultaneously satisfied rules on correct high-complexity items.
new_measurements_proposed.how_much_to_collect: >=6 items whose distractors are orthogonally keyed to individual rules, spanning 1 to 4 co-acting rules near the child's edge.

tail_precision_rationale: M-DIFFREACH under adaptive rule-count escalation is the single sharpest tail statistic - it walks each child to the exact number of co-acting rules they can bind before failing. M-ERRTYPE reads the chosen distractor against a per-rule violation key, so a near-miss (correct on 2 of 3 rules) marks latent ability just below the cut and separates it from random error. M-RTFIRST captures reflective encoding (able solvers look longer before the first tap) and M-REV distinguishes confident single placements from guess-and-check, turning one hard matrix into a rule-resolved ability estimate rather than a single right/wrong bit.
age_rationale: K-1 gets 2x2 single-rule items with large tap tiles and snap-to-cell placement (no fine drag, no reading), matching limited fine-motor precision and pre-literacy. 2-3 adds a second rule and 3x3 grids; 4-5 and 6-8 add abstraction, arithmetic/logical rules, and perceptually confusable distractors. The same shell spans all bands purely by rule count and abstraction.

adaptive.content_range: single-rule 2x2 figural completion (K-1) up to 3-4 co-acting-rule 3x3 abstract matrices with arithmetic/logical relations (6-8 tail)
difficulty_levers: grid size 2x2 to 3x3
number of simultaneous rules 1 to 4
rule type constant to progression to distribution-of-three to arithmetic to XOR/AND/OR
attribute count and type (shape, color, size, number, position, rotation)
perceptual similarity of distractors
option count 4 to 6
adaptive.notes: Fully procedurally generable from a rule x attribute grammar with distractors keyed to individual rule violations; supports a bottomless above-level bank for ceiling probing and parallel clones for consistency checks.

engagement_hook: Powering up a machine - the correct tile makes gears spin and lights cascade for an immediate juicy success cue, and escalating rule complexity feels like unlocking harder levels.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Guard perceptual load (keep distractor similarity a deliberate lever, not accidental noise); avoid color-only rules by pairing color with shape/pattern for color-vision differences; big snap-to-cell tiles remove motor-precision demands; ghost-hand plus warm-up neutralizes game-novelty variance; do not over-reward speed since reflective latency is expected on hard items. Reading policy (D-017): reading is a REQUIRED baseline-literacy capability, not a construct-irrelevant risk to mitigate — instructions and stimuli are on-screen text only (never audio); K-1 uses very simple, high-frequency words a beginning reader can interpret; a child who cannot read the grade-appropriate text is intentionally screened out (capability-to-benefit from reading-based Timeback).

name: Build the Tile
topics_techniques_covered: figural_matrix: 3x3 matrix completion where the missing tile is CONSTRUCTED rather than selected from options
figural_matrix: Raven-like relational rules running across rows and columns
figural_matrix: abstract colored shapes varying by shape/color/size/position
figural_matrix: RPM rule taxonomy - constant-in-a-row, progression, distribution-of-three, arithmetic add/subtract of a numeric attribute
figural_matrix: cognitive-model-driven difficulty (rule count x abstraction x perceptual load)
matrix_induction: derive each attribute of the missing cell from co-acting row/column rules
visual_rule_discovery: full content-range coverage across this type's difficulty spectrum (recat full-range retag)
one_liner: Instead of picking a tile, the child BUILDS the missing matrix cell by setting its shape, color and number so every row and column rule holds.
interaction: A 2x2 or 3x3 matrix shows the bottom-right cell empty. Below sit attribute pickers: a row of shape buttons, a row of color swatches, and a count stepper (1-3 dots). Tapping a picker updates a live preview tile that appears in the empty cell. The child sets each attribute (any order, can change freely) then taps GO to submit the constructed tile. No option tray, no typing, no reading.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand sweeps a row then a column of the empty cell (showing where the rules meet), taps the correct shape, the correct color, then the correct count; the preview tile assembles live and the matrix glows. One unscored single-attribute 2x2 warm-up (set only the shape) runs before scoring.

learning_science.why: Producing an answer rather than recognizing one yields deeper encoding and blocks recognition-only guessing, so the score reflects genuine rule derivation.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The child constructs the tile attribute-by-attribute instead of choosing among ready-made options, so each attribute must be independently derived.
learning_science.source: Slamecka & Graf (1978), Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Learning and Memory 4(6)

learning_science.why: Matrix difficulty is set by how many relations must be bound at once, the true tail driver.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Each attribute (shape, color, count) carries its own row/column rule, so the number of co-acting rules the child resolves is read directly from which attributes are correct.
learning_science.source: Halford, Wilson & Phillips (1998), Behavioral and Brain Sciences 21(6)

learning_science.principle: Process account of the Raven Progressive Matrices
learning_science.why: RPM ability is rule induction plus goal management over a fixed rule taxonomy.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Attributes are governed by the constant/progression/distribution-of-three/arithmetic rule set so construction taps the same induction RPM measures.
learning_science.source: Carpenter, Just & Shell (1990), Psychological Review 97(3)

learning_science.why: A constructed multi-attribute answer yields graded evidence from one rich item.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Scoring is per-attribute-correct (0..k) so a tile right on 2 of 3 attributes earns graded credit and behaves like several dichotomous items.
learning_science.source: Embretson & Reise (2000), Item Response Theory for Psychologists

tail_precision_rationale: Because the tile is CONSTRUCTED, M-POLY reads exactly which of the co-acting attribute-rules the child satisfied, and M-RULEID reports the maximum simultaneously-satisfied rules - a per-child relational-complexity ceiling that a single right/wrong bit cannot expose. M-ERRTYPE names the specific attribute-rule missed (a color-progression slip vs a count-arithmetic slip), so a near-miss at high complexity marks latent ability just below the cut. M-PATH (order of attribute settings) plus M-RTFIRST distinguish a child who derives each attribute deliberately from one who flails; guessing is near-impossible because there is no option set to eliminate, making high-difficulty accuracy unusually clean tail evidence.
age_rationale: Constructing a tile requires holding several partial rule-results in mind and executing multiple coordinated picker taps, which exceeds K-1 working-memory and fine-motor limits; K-1 figural_matrix is served by the selection-based FLU-MATRIX-01. 2-3 constructs on a single attribute (shape) with a 2x2 grid; 4-5 adds color; 6-8 adds count/arithmetic and 3x3 grids with up to three co-acting rules. Large picker buttons and a live preview keep motor demands modest from grade 2 up.

adaptive.content_range: single-attribute 2x2 construction (grades 2-3) up to 3-attribute 3x3 construction with arithmetic/distribution rules (6-8 tail)
difficulty_levers: grid size 2x2 to 3x3
number of attributes to construct 1 to 3
rule type constant to progression to distribution-of-three to arithmetic
abstractness of shapes
count range for the numeric attribute
adaptive.notes: Fully procedurally generable from a rule x attribute grammar; the answer key is the attribute vector so per-attribute scoring and parallel clones for consistency checks are automatic; supports a bottomless above-level bank for ceiling probing.

engagement_hook: You are the tile-maker: forging the missing piece attribute-by-attribute and watching the machine light up when your built tile is right feels more agentive than picking from a menu.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Pair color with shape so color-vision differences never decide an item; keep picker buttons large to remove fine-motor load; live preview and undo prevent slip errors; ghost-hand plus warm-up neutralizes construction-novelty variance; cap attribute count for young bands so working memory does not confound rule derivation; do not over-reward speed since deliberate construction is expected. Reading policy (D-017): reading is a REQUIRED baseline-literacy capability, not a construct-irrelevant risk to mitigate — instructions and stimuli are on-screen text only (never audio); K-1 uses very simple, high-frequency words a beginning reader can interpret; a child who cannot read the grade-appropriate text is intentionally screened out (capability-to-benefit from reading-based Timeback).

name: Odd Pair Out
topics_techniques_covered: figure_analogy: each pair shows A turning into B by a transformation; the child compares the transformation ACROSS pairs (a relation between relations) rather than completing one analogy
figure_analogy: A:B relations of one clear change (size, rotation, count, shade) and two-change combined rules for older bands
odd_one_out: among several same-rule pairs one pair follows a different transformation; select the pair that breaks the shared relation
visual_rule_discovery: infer the transformation each pair encodes and detect the one that is inconsistent with the majority
figure_classification: full content-range coverage across this type's difficulty spectrum (recat full-range retag)
one_liner: Several before-and-after pairs all change in the same secret way except one; the child taps the pair whose change is different.
interaction: Four (K-8: up to five) pairs are shown, each a left figure with an arrow to its transformed right figure. Three or more pairs share one transformation (e.g., turn 90 degrees, or add a dot); exactly one pair uses a different transformation. The child taps the odd pair (the whole pair highlights) and confirms with a check; an optional confidence tap (sure / not sure) follows on a subset of items. Exactly one selection is scored per item.
self_teach: The ghost-hand sweeps left-to-right along each pair's arrow (tracing the change), pauses on the three matching pairs with a soft same-chime, then lands on the mismatching pair, which pulses and is tapped. The warm-up uses a vivid single change (all pairs get bigger except one that gets smaller) so the compare-the-change idea is obvious wordlessly.

learning_science.why: Judging whether two transformations are the same is second-order relational processing, a core driver of fluid-reasoning difficulty and of the gifted tail.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The task requires binding each pair's relation and then comparing relations, and difficulty scales with the number of dimensions the relation spans (Halford's relational complexity).
learning_science.source: Halford, Wilson & Phillips (1998), Behavioral and Brain Sciences 21(6)

learning_science.why: Detecting the odd pair requires aligning relational structure, not surface features, which is the essence of analogical reasoning.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Distractor pairs share surface features but differ in relation, so surface matching fails and only structural alignment succeeds.
learning_science.source: Gentner (1983), Cognitive Science 7(2)

learning_science.why: The shared rule is never stated; the child must abstract it from multiple instances and use it as a comparison standard.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Three consistent pairs provide the inductive basis; the fourth tests whether the abstracted rule was correctly formed.
learning_science.source: Holyoak & Thagard (1995), Mental Leaps

tail_precision_rationale: M-RULEID captures how many relational dimensions the shared transformation spanned on correctly solved items (a same-turn rule vs a turn-and-shade rule), exposing the relational complexity a child can bind at once - a cleaner tail separator than a single difficulty index. M-ERRTYPE distinguishes a near-miss (child locked onto a surface feature and chose a plausible foil) from a random error, flagging latent ability just below threshold, and M-CONF adds metacognitive calibration to down-weight lucky guesses at the cut. M-RTFIRST indexes reflective encoding before the first tap.
age_rationale: Comparing a change across pairs requires abstracting a relation and holding it as a standard, which is fragile in K-1; the youngest band is covered by the direct analogy and odd-one-out FLU types. 2-3 uses one salient change with four pairs; 4-5 adds less salient single changes; 6-8 uses combined two-change relations and five pairs. Answering is a single large tap, so motor demand is minimal.

adaptive.content_range: one salient single-change relation among four pairs (grades 2-3) up to combined multi-dimension relations among five pairs (6-8)
difficulty_levers: number of relational dimensions in the shared rule
salience and type of the odd pair's deviation
surface similarity between odd and matching pairs (foil pull)
number of pairs shown
perceptual load per figure
adaptive.notes: Pairs are generated from a transformation grammar; the odd pair is produced by swapping one transformation parameter, and a check confirms exactly one pair deviates, giving high-throughput cloning.

engagement_hook: A spot-the-impostor puzzle: three changes are secretly twins and one is a copycat that got it wrong - catching the fake change is a satisfying gotcha.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Guarantee exactly one pair deviates and that the deviation is relational (not a mere size/render artifact) so M-RULEID is valid; balance the odd pair's position to avoid position bias; pair color with shape so the shared rule never relies on color alone; ghost-hand plus warm-up controls the novel compare-the-change format; keep confidence taps optional to avoid burden. Reading policy (D-017): reading is a REQUIRED baseline-literacy capability, not a construct-irrelevant risk to mitigate — instructions and stimuli are on-screen text only (never audio); K-1 uses very simple, high-frequency words a beginning reader can interpret; a child who cannot read the grade-appropriate text is intentionally screened out (capability-to-benefit from reading-based Timeback).

name: Stack the Panel
topics_techniques_covered: figural_matrix: logical relations (XOR, OR, AND, consistent union) over attributes where the third cell in a row is the superposition/combination of the first two
figural_matrix: Raven-like relational rules running across rows and columns
figural_matrix: RPM figure-addition and figure-subtraction rules (combine or cancel marks across a row)
figural_matrix: cognitive-model-driven difficulty (rule count x abstraction x perceptual load) across the full K-8 range
matrix_induction: derive the missing cell by applying a logical combination rule inferred from complete rows
visual_rule_discovery: full content-range coverage across this type's difficulty spectrum (recat full-range retag)
one_liner: The child figures out how two panels in a row combine into the third, then picks the panel that correctly stacks the last row together.
interaction: Each row shows three cells, where the third cell is the logical combination (overlay/union, exclusive-or, or intersection) of the first two cells' marks on a small shared grid. The top rows are shown complete to reveal the rule; the bottom row shows its first two cells and an empty third cell with 4-6 candidate panels in a tray. The child taps a candidate to snap it into the empty cell (tap another to swap), then taps GO to submit. One confirmed selection is the answer; no typing, no reading.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand hovers the two filled cells of a complete row, slides them together so their marks visibly merge into the third cell (the overlay lighting up), then drops the matching tray panel into the empty cell of the last row and the stack glows. One unscored warm-up (two single dots merging into a two-dot panel) runs before scoring begins.

learning_science.principle: Process account of the Raven Progressive Matrices (figure addition/subtraction)
learning_science.why: A large share of hard RPM items are governed by superposition and figure addition/subtraction rules that require combining whole cells, a distinct and demanding operation from attribute progression.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Every item is generated from an explicit logical-combination rule (OR/XOR/AND) applied cell-to-cell, and distractors are keyed to specific combination errors (union instead of XOR, one source omitted).
learning_science.source: Carpenter, Just & Shell (1990), Psychological Review 97(3)

learning_science.why: Difficulty is set by how many marks/relations must be bound and combined simultaneously.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Difficulty escalates by the number of marks combined and by stacking a second attribute grid, so the ceiling probes combination capacity, not clutter.
learning_science.source: Halford, Wilson & Phillips (1998), Behavioral and Brain Sciences 21(6)

learning_science.principle: Cognitive load theory - minimize extraneous load
learning_science.why: Written rules would add extraneous load that masks the combining operation being measured.
learning_science.concrete_decision: A wordless ghost-hand merge animation and snap-to-cell tiles carry all instruction so working memory is spent on the combination rule.
learning_science.source: Sweller, van Merrienboer & Paas (1998), Educational Psychology Review 10(3)

tail_precision_rationale: M-DIFFREACH under adaptive escalation of the combination rule (single OR up to XOR stacked over two attribute grids) walks each child to the exact combination complexity they can bind before failing - the sharpest single tail statistic for this shell. M-ERRTYPE reads the chosen distractor against a combination-error key (union-for-XOR, dropped-source, intersection-for-union), so a near-miss marks latent ability just below the cut and separates it from random error.
